passage: Note, Arnab, class teacher. Lopa read me a line from the letter she wrote to her grandmother, who died in January. On her grandmother's birthday, Lopa told me, the family lit a lamp on the balcony, and she cooked her grandmother's favourite khichdi with her mother and cousins, following a recipe in her grandmother's handwriting. She said the kitchen smelled like Nani's kitchen, and everyone laughed and cried in the same minute. She plans to do it every year. I asked whether she would like me to keep an eye on her school workload in April. She said she was fine, and thanked me. I will check in quietly, and I'm glad she has found her own way of staying close to her grandmother.

qa.a: Lopa cooked her grandmother's favourite khichdi.

qa.q: What was Lopa feeling when everyone laughed and cried in the same minute?
qa.a: Lopa was feeling bittersweet, sad and comforted together, since the kitchen smelled like Nani's kitchen.

qa.q: What else could Lopa add to her remembrance?
qa.a: Lopa could keep writing letters or look at photos or visit a place her grandmother loved, since more small rituals give the bond a lasting home.

qa.q: How might Lopa's mother see the day?
qa.a: Lopa's mother probably feels comforted to share the memory with her family, since they cooked, laughed and cried together.

grounding: A teen writes a letter to her grandmother, lights a lamp on her birthday and cooks her favourite dish with the family, keeping the bond alive.

passage:
14 January
Biji would have been seventy-eight today.
This morning I wrote her a letter. I told her about my science marks, the new calf at Mamaji's farm, how Mummy still hums her songs while cooking. I folded it into her old prayer book.
In the evening we lit a diya by her photo, Mummy, Papa, Veer and me. Nobody said much, but nobody left either.
Then we made her kadhi. Mummy read out Biji's handwritten recipe and I stirred, and it split because I stopped stirring, just like Biji always warned. We all laughed. My friend Kishore came by with his mother, and we fed them too.
I think we'll do this every year. The letter, the diya, the kadhi. It feels like she's still in the kitchen with us, a little.
Amandeep

qa.q: Where did Amandeep put the letter?
qa.a: Amandeep folded it into Biji's old prayer book.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when the kadhi split?
qa.a: Amandeep felt a warm, bittersweet closeness, laughing with the family because Biji had always warned about exactly that.

qa.q: What else could keep this tradition meaningful as the years pass?
qa.a: The family could let each person add something, like a memory read aloud, so the ritual grows with them.

qa.q: How might Mummy experience the day?
qa.a: Mummy, who still hums Biji's songs, gets to remember her mother openly with the family, reading the recipe and laughing together.

grounding: Shows a teen writing a letter to a dead grandmother, lighting a lamp on her birthday and cooking her dish with the family as a lasting remembrance.

Vidya: it's Ammamma's birthday on Sunday. first one without her
Hrithik: I know. my mom's been quiet all week
Vidya: I want to do something. not just all of us being sad in separate rooms
Hrithik: like what
Vidya: I wrote her a letter last night. about the mango pickle and how she cheated at pallanguzhi
Hrithik: she totally did
Vidya: I want to read it out on Sunday. then light the lamp near her photo
Hrithik: and food?
Vidya: her paruppu urundai kuzhambu. Amma has the recipe in Ammamma's handwriting
Hrithik: I'll come early and do the grinding. she always made me do it
Vidya: deal. and maybe we do this every year
Hrithik: yes. like she's still in charge of us

qa.a: About the mango pickle and how she cheated at pallanguzhi.

qa.q: What does Vidya want for Sunday, and why?
